newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MINISTERS SEE NEW ERA OF HUNGARIAN-ROMANIAN TIES.
newsitem.headline: MINISTERS SEE NEW ERA OF HUNGARIAN-ROMANIAN TIES.

text.p: Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told Hungary on Friday a new era in long-strained Hungarian-Romanian ties had begun.
"We are on the verge of a new chapter of bilateral ties," Severin told a news conference after exchanging ratified basic treaty documents with his Hungarian counterpart, Laszlo Kovacs.

The treaty, signed in September, aims to end old quarrels by guaranteeing Romania's western borders and ensuring the rights of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians and is seen as vital to the ambitions of Romania and Hungary to move closer to Europe and NATO.

Severin, on his first foreign visit since his appointment, said Romanian elections which brought a new government to power last month had set the conditions for marked improvement in relations with Hungary,
"Conditions to implement the basic treaty are now given," he said.

As the first concrete steps towards better relations, Kovacs and Severin agreed on reopening the Romanian consulate in Debrecen and the Hungarian consulate in Cluj, both closed during Romania's communist Ceausescu-regime.
Honorary consulates will also be set up in the Romanian Black Sea port of Constanta and the Hungarian town of Gyor.
The two ministers said that bilateral agreements on free trade and joint action to fight organised crime will be signed shortly.

Ties between Budapest and Bucharest had long been tense, mainly because of disputes over the status of ethnic Hungarians and because Romanian nationalists suspected Budapest of designs on Transylvania, once ruled by Austro-Hungary.
Kovacs said the two nations must now achieve a better understanding of each other and bilateral relations have to be based on mutual trust.
"Trust was the word that came up most frequently during our meeting," Kovacs said. "Trust needs to be established between the two nations, between ethnic majorities and ethnic minorities."
After the fall of communism in 1989, Romania's ethnic Hungarians' demands for more rights met stiff opposition from the former leftist cabinet, which included nationalist parties.
Victory by centrist parties in November polls and the inclusion of ethnic Hungarians in the new government -- a first in post-communist Romania -- brought a change of mood.
"The fact that my first visit led to Hungary shows the importance we attribute to bilateral ties and also our hope for an effective and long-lasting partnership," Severin said.
Severin said that while very important, the basic treaty is but the first step on a long road the two countries are committed to follow.
"A basic treaty is only important when relations are strained. When they are good, there is no need for a treaty," he said.
During his three-day stay in Hungary Severin also met Prime Minister Gyula Horn and President Arpad Goncz and will meet representatives of Hungary's Romanian minority.
